We are the ones overlooked, the underdogs who started with nothing but curiosity, ambition, and the willingness to learn. We may not have the strongest backgrounds or the most impressive track records, but we refuse to let our starting point define our destination. We are here to challenge ourselves, build things that matter, and prove that extraordinary things can come from ordinary beginnings.

We will grow together, take risks, and turn ambitious ideas into reality.
summary:
Project Human Frontier is a browser-based lunar outpost survival game that helps children ages 7–12 understand real engineering trade-offs in space exploration. During a 32-Sol mission, players balance power, water, life support, radiation protection, crew health, and scientific exploration.

The game transforms NASA open data into meaningful decisions rather than passive facts. Curated NASA DONKI space-weather records affect radiation, equipment reliability, and rover risk, while LRO Diviner, LOLA, and OSDR RadLab resources ground the lunar environment and science explanations. Every choice has a cost: protecting a rover may consume power needed to recycle water or protect the crew.

Guided onboarding, plain-language STEM debriefs, bilingual support, and replayable outcomes make complex mission-planning concepts accessible and engaging. The project is free, browser-playable, requires no account, and helps young learners understand how science and engineering decisions determine mission success.
details:
WHAT WE BUILT

Project Human Frontier is an interactive, browser-based lunar outpost mission trainer designed for children ages 7–12. Players take command of an Artemis-inspired outpost and attempt to keep four crew members safe throughout a 32-Sol campaign.

The experience focuses on the engineering trade-offs that determine whether a deep-space mission succeeds or fails. Players must balance electrical power, water recovery, life support, radiation protection, crew health, communications, and scientific exploration. The objective is not simply to find one correct answer. Every useful action consumes time, energy, equipment, or another limited resource.

Figure 1 — The interactive mission cockpit allows players to monitor essential resources, crew condition, space weather, and station systems from one interface.

HOW IT WORKS

Each Sol follows a guided mission-control cycle. Players review the morning briefing and NASA space-weather conditions, respond to mission events, assign crew members, manage station systems and rover expeditions, allocate food and water, and then complete the Sol.

At the end of each Sol, the simulation calculates the consequences of the player’s decisions. A STEM debrief explains what happened, why it happened, and what the player could try differently. The same mission seed and decisions always produce the same result, allowing outcomes to be replayed, compared, and verified.

A signature example is the Sol 7 “Golden Crisis.” The player must choose between preserving valuable rover science data and prioritizing the habitat’s water-recovery system. Protecting the rover consumes power and may reduce the water available to the crew. Prioritizing water protects the habitat but may sacrifice scientific progress. Neither decision is free, and both produce visible consequences.

Figure 2 — The Sol 7 Golden Crisis demonstrates a genuine engineering trade-off between protecting the crew’s water supply and preserving rover science data.

NASA DATA INTEGRATION

NASA data is a functional component of the simulation rather than a decorative reference.

Players can select one of three curated 32-day space-weather timelines derived from NASA DONKI records. These datasets include solar flares, coronal mass ejections, solar energetic particle events, and interplanetary shocks. Their severity affects radiation accumulation, equipment reliability, rover incident risk, repair probability, and solar-array performance.

NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Diviner data informs the educational lunar thermal profile, while LOLA products provide terrain and South Polar location context. NASA OSDR RadLab radiation measurements provide a reference for the background radiation model. NASA ECLSS resources inform the game’s oxygen, carbon-dioxide removal, and water-recovery concepts.

Figure 3 — Players choose a mission profile derived from archived NASA DONKI space-weather observations, producing different risk patterns and replayable outcomes.

The application identifies whether information is observed, inferred, or simulated. Archived NASA measurements are preserved as source data, while gameplay coefficients and compressed time scales are clearly treated as educational abstractions. The game does not present static archived data as a live forecast.

EDUCATIONAL IMPACT AND CREATIVITY

Many educational space products explain individual facts but do not allow children to experience how mission systems affect one another. Project Human Frontier turns those relationships into gameplay.

A decision that saves power today may reduce water recovery tomorrow. A rover expedition may increase scientific progress while placing additional demand on power, communications, and crew time. Radiation shielding can protect astronaut health but leaves less energy available for other mission objectives.

Guided onboarding, contextual hints, plain-language science explanations, and forgiving failure conditions help young players learn through experimentation. Victory, defeat, and different decision branches encourage replay without treating failure as punishment.

The project can support independent learning, family play, and classroom discussion. Its intended impact is to help young learners understand that space exploration depends on systems thinking, evidence, planning, and responsible decision-making.

TECHNOLOGY, ACCESSIBILITY, AND SAFETY

The application was developed with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and a deterministic client-side simulation engine. Automated tests verify resource conservation, NASA data catalogs, campaign outcomes, save recovery, responsive behavior, and accessibility requirements.

The game includes English and Vietnamese localization, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support, contextual help, responsive layouts, and large mobile touch targets. It runs directly in a web browser, requires no download or user account, and does not collect personal information or analytics.
